subsubtopic: WATER LEVELS IN THE GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
I wish to point out that while I spoke a year ago today on the question of water levels on the Great Lakes, I wish tonight to draw the attention of the House to a situation that applies to one lake only in the Great Lakes system, and that is Lake Ontario, where the water level has reached a point that it has become a problem for the Province of Ontario, the State of New York, and even for the two nations that border on the Great Lakes.
At the present time there is an investigation being held into water levels on the Great Lakes, as a direct result of the comments made a year ago following a private Member's bill. But I say to you that the question of controlling the water level of Lake Ontario is not intertwined with the problem of controlling the water levels of Lake Erie, Lake Huron, Lake Michigan and Lake Superior. If one spreads his attention to the water level problem of the Great Lakes, on all five lakes concerned, he is going to be wasting time regarding the problem of Lake Ontario, because Lake Ontario can be controlled at the present time if action were to be taken.
Lake Superior is under control at the present time, and has been since 1921 when the International Joint Commission took control of it and has maintained its level within a range of four feet for more than 40 years. In fact at the present time the water level of Lake Superior is confined to a range of only 18 inches. It varies in height above sea level from 602.1 feet to 603.6 feet, which is a mere range of 18 inches on the greatest of the Great Lakes.
May 11. 1965	COMMONS
The water levels of Lake Huron, Lake Michigan and Lake Erie are not controlled in any manner at the present time, but when you come down to the last of the Great Lakes, Lake Ontario, you have a body of water that is segregated from the other lakes by the great Niagara Falls, where you have a drop of 168 feet, to say nothing of the drop in the rapids section above the falls and the rapids section below the falls.
Lake Ontario, being isolated from the other Great Lakes, should be considered absolutely independently of the others when consideration is given to the problem of water levels. Now, in considering water levels one has to go back to the basic bedrock of the whole control system, and that is the international treaty, signed in 1909, between the United States and Great Britain on behalf of Canada. It was as a direct result of that treaty that the International Joint Commission, as we know it today, was set up. Its first major activity, following its establishment in 1911, was the regulation and control of Lake Superior, which it has been able to control to the satisfaction of all concerned.
The important point to bear in mind in this treaty between the United States and Great Britain on behalf of Canada, which governs the international boundary waters, is article 8, and I maintain that this international treaty is being violated every day of the week and every week of the year, and no action is being taken to enforce that treaty despite the fact that it was signed on Canada's behalf by one of the most brilliant negotiators the world has ever seen, Lord Bryce.
In article 8 of the treaty there is an agreement between the United States and Canada, through the British government, which states:
The High Contracting Parties shall have, each on its own side of the boundary, equal and similar rights in the use of the waters hereinbefore defined as boundary waters.
The following order of precedence shall be observed among the various uses enumerated hereinafter for these waters, and no use shall be permitted which tends materially to conflict with or restrain any other use which is given preference over it in this order of precedence:
(1)	Uses for domestic and sanitary purposes;
(2)	Uses for navigation, including the service of canals for the purposes of navigation;
(3)	Uses for power and for irrigation purposes
I wish to stress as strongly as I can that water used for domestic and sanitary purposes is given No. 1 priority or precedence. Water to be used for navigation is given second precedence, and the third or last precedence is for water power and irrigation
DEBATES	1177
Water Levels of Great Lakes purposes. If this treaty were being observed to the letter, as I maintain international treaties should be observed when Canada signs them or her representative signs them, we would not have the trouble on Lake Ontario that we are having today.
There is no shortage of water. There is certainly and definitely a shortage of regulation. The problem in connection with Lake Ontario is simply that more water is being allowed to flow out of it than comes into the lake.
There are three major sources of inflow to the lake, the greatest one of course being the Niagara River, which empties all the waters of the Great Lakes down into Lake Ontario. The second great source of water for Lake Ontario is the inflow of such rivers as the Trent, the Moira, the Cataraqui, the Humber, the Don and other rivers that flow into the lake, the Genesee on the south side, and then you have rainfall and snow.
From that sum total of the inflow from Lake Erie, plus the inflow from other rivers and lakes flowing into Lake Ontario, plus rainfall and snow, you have an ample supply of water to keep Lake Ontario at any level man may desire, if the control dams at Iroquois, Ontario, or at Cornwall, Ontario, should be operated with the intention of controlling the level of Lake Ontario.
But unfortunately the powerhouse at Cornwall has been erected with no thought of controlling the water level of Lake Ontario, but primarily with the thought in mind of developing as much electric power through the use of water as it is humanly possible to generate from the waters flowing through the St. Lawrence River.
I have in my hand a yellow or orange covered book which is entitled, "The Regulation of Lake Ontario, Plan 1958D." This book is the report to the International Joint Commission by the International St. Lawrence River Board of Control. This is the book by which the International St. Lawrence River Board of Control operates the canal system, the locks, the dams and the power houses on the St. Lawrence River between Kingston and Montreal.
This book is the bible for the operation of the river as I have mentioned, and I regret exceedingly that the book does not observe the terms of the treaty where precedence is established for the use of water as from 1909. This treaty of 1909 may be 56 years old, but the signatory for Great Britain on behalf of Canada was, as I said before, one of the greatest minds the world has ever seen,
May 11, 1965

Water Levels of Great Lakes Viscount Lord Bryce, and the man who negotiated for the United States was one of the greatest statesmen they have produced, Elihu Root, Secretary of State in three different cabinets of the United States and a man who must have been of great ability and integrity because in 1912, which is something like 53 years ago, he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. Mr. Root considered the proper evaluation of the uses of water and came up with the three divisions I have mentioned to you. Those three divisions are true and sufficient for all time.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
It is not necessary to add anything to that three-part table; but I would point out to you that the Oxford English Dictionary defines "precedent" as, "a thing or person that precedes or goes before another". Notice the word "precedes". And the Oxford English Dictionary states that "precedes" means "to go before or beyond another in quality or degree; to surpass, excel; to exceed". But if you look at the control statements prepared by Government employees who are endeavouring to operate the St. Lawrence River system, you will find reference time after time to treating all the users of water "equitably". "Let us treat them on a compromise basis". "Let us treat them equally". The table of precedence in the International Boundary Waters Agreement does not say "to treat the users of water equitably" or "on a compromise basis"; it says that they shall be treated on this basis of precedence.
When looking at the operation of the St. Lawrence system one has to consider the low water that is resulting in Lake Ontario as a direct result of the operations now being conducted on that stream. It is more than passing strange that these Parliament Buildings are in a position to overlook the operation of the Ottawa River which is dammed in many places for power development purposes; the Rideau Canal, which is dammed in many places in order to control it for navigation purposes; and the St. Lawrence River, which is within 60 miles of the Parliament Buildings. Here below Parliament Hill you can look down upon the Rideau River with its dams and controls. The water is maintained at an even level and the canals are made navigable by maintaining a certain depth of water during the navigation season. The Ottawa River, which is below Parliament Hill here, is controlled by the Quebec hydroelectric power dam at Carillon, or Point Fortune, and controls a body of water 60 miles in length from

Carillon right back to the Chaudiere Falls just west of the Parliament Buildings.
But what do you find if you look 60 miles to the south down toward Cornwall, Prescott or Johnstown? You find the third side of the triangle where the water is running as free as the day the world was created; as free as it ever ran in history. Yet we are told that Lake Ontario is under control.
I have in my hand a copy of the official application of the Government of Canada to the International Joint Commission in 1952. I see that the Government of Canada was asking the International Joint Commission for the right to proceed with the development of power works on the St. Lawrence River. There are many, many phrases in this application of the Government of Canada, but there are one or two that I wish to draw to your attention specifically. We find this. The application, in paragraph 10, subsection (c), of the Government of Canada asks the International Joint Commission for permission to build these works and says:
Subject to the provisions of paragraph (e) of this section, the flow through the International Rapids Section in any period shall equal the discharge from Lake Ontario as determined for that period in accordance with Method of Regulation No. 5 referred to in paragraph (b) of this section and this flow shall be maintained uniformly throughout that period.
That is a lot of words of which the substance is that the flow of water in the St. Lawrence River after the power development works are installed shall be as great as it ever was before. Why, in the name of heaven would you build a dam at Iroquois and build a powerhouse at Cornwall, both of which are capable of holding Lake Ontario at a predetermined level, if you did not intend to use them? But here we are told:
Subject to the provisions of paragraph (e) of this section, the flow through the International Rapids section in any period shall equal the discharge from Lake Ontario as determined for that period in accordance with Method of Regulation No. 5-
In this interesting application we are also told in subsection (a) that "the works shall be operated and maintained in conformity with the requirements of the prior rights and interests of navigation on the St. Lawrence River." It does not say whether these prior rights of navigation are for the people downstream on the St. Lawrence or upstream; it refers to the prior rights of navigation on the St. Lawrence River. At least in this application, in these words it is admitted that navigation has a prior right on the use of
May 11, 1965

water, over power. But it goes on to make this very amazing statement:
-and in such manner as to protect the rights and interests of others engaged in the development of power in the river below the International Rapids section.
I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the use of that word "below". On any stream of water, the people on the upside have prior rights over the people on the downside. The St. Lawrence River is downside from the Great Lakes, which are the headwaters or source of the St. Lawrence River. Those people who live in the basin of the Great Lakes have prior rights and prior claims to the use of the water in the Great Lakes system over and above anybody on the downside, or downstream, end of the water. But this application to the International Joint Commission, section 10, subsection (a) has that amazing clause in it:
The works (shall be built) in such a manner as to protect the rights and Interests of others engaged in the development of power in the river below the International Rapids Section.
The amusing thing-and I am making a change here from "amazing" to "amusing"- in this application is that the Canadian application has 14 clauses in it; the American application to the same International Joint Commission has 17 clauses in it. The first 11 sections are exactly the same in making their application to the International Joint Commission; but from section 12 on to No. 17 the American application differs in several important respects from the Canadian Government's application. It is interesting that in section 10 of both the Canadian application and the American Government's application we have the phrase appearing that they will give consideration to the "development of power in the river below the International Rapids section and in such a manner as to protect the rights and interests of others engaged in the development of power in the river below the International Rapids Section". It is interesting in this way; that the clause might as well read that in the eighth day of every week we will do so-and-so with the river. There is not an eighth day in the week, as anyone knows, and I would like to emphasize to you that there are no prior rights for people downstream. But it is in this application of the Canadian Government, and appears in the American government's application. Don't think that this makes the use of "prior downstream rights" legal, because an interesting angle comes up in the American application beyond paragraph 11;

Water Levels of Great Lakes because immediately thereafter, in paragraph 13, the Americans say:
In submitting this application, the United States expressly reserves all its existing rights in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River including among others the rights mutually extended to the United States and Canada under the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909-
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
You will see that the Americans are not releasing any rights to downstream residents, and after having willingly put clause 10 into their application, they point out in clause 13-this clause does not appear in the Canadian application-that in submitting this application the United States expressly reserves its existing rights in the Great Lakes. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the existing rights of Canadian residents on the Canadian side of the Great Lakes remain and are the same in 1965 as they were prior to 1952. But the Canadian Government's application does not spell it out the way the smart Americans spell theirs out, after having signed these amusing and amazing clauses that, when establishing the power developments on the St. Lawrence, they would protect the rights and interests of those engaged in the development of power below the International Rapids section.
After these two applications had been received by the International Joint Commission they considered the matter for a short while and then issued a permit to the two Governments to participate in the power development of the St. Lawrence River. In their granting of the rights to develop the power on the St. Lawrence River we find an interesting situation. I have before me the permission granted by the International Joint Commission, and in section (c) on page 3 we read this:
The works shall be constructed, maintained and operated in such manner as to safeguard the rights and lawful interests of others engaged or to be engaged in the development of power in the St. Lawrence River below the International Rapids section.
Then the International Joint Commission says in this formal order:
The works shall be so designed, constructed, maintained and operated as to safeguard so far as possible the rights of all interests-
I point out that this is in open conflict with the International Treaty of 1909, which establishes a table of precedence in which domestic and sanitary purposes is in number one position, navigation is in number two position, and water power and irrigation in number three position. But that does not stop
May 11, 1965

Water Levels of Great Lakes the International Joint Commission from issuing an order that the works on the St. Lawrence shall be so designed, constructed, maintained and operated as to safeguard so far as possible the rights of all interests affected by the level of the St. Lawrence. It makes no reference to the table of precedence as established by the international agreement, as it should have done.
So we have a situation where people are complaining of the low water in Lake Ontario because of the trouble they have in putting their boats into the lake in the summertime. We have complaints from the municipalities because the suction pipes to draw in the water are in shallow water today rather than in the deep water the municipalities have come to expect. We have complaints from the shipping people that they have to light load their bottoms for the simple reason that if they load them to the 25J foot draught, about which we do a lot of talking, they are going to scrape the bottoms of their boats in the lakes and in local harbours, and damage will be done to the boats. This despite the fact that navigation is given second precedence in the table of precedence. And when it comes to the power users we have to give that matter very serious thought.
In the manipulation of the levels of Lake Ontario we are told-and it is a fact at the present time-that efforts are made to control the low and high levels of the lake. In the summer months from April to December they are controlled between 244 feet and 248 feet as nearly as may be. In aiming at this figure in the navigation season of 244 feet up to 248 feet it is thought that this will give boats coming into Lake Ontario all the depth they require. I am assured by officials of the Toronto Harbour Commission that a height above sea level of 244 feet will allow the boats to come into Toronto harbour with a 25i foot draught, as promised in all seaway speeches, in a 27 foot channel. But once the navigation season is over-and this is generally unknown to the public-these control figures for Lake Ontario are changed and the level of the lake goes down. We are told that in the wintertime they endeavour to control Lake Ontario between a level of 248.05 feet on the high side, and 243.07 feet on the low side, which is a range of over four feet.
The interesting thing about letting the water level down to 243.07 feet is that boats which are tied up in Hamilton harbour, or Toronto harbour, or Rochester harbour, or

Oswego reach the bottom of the harbour when the Lake Ontario level is lowered, a fact generally unknown to the people on the shores. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that when the average level of Lake Ontario has been 246 feet for 105 years, according to Government records, we should not go below that average level of 246 feet. We can justify a figure of 246 feet above sea level because this has been the average for 105 years. Property owners around the shore of Lake Ontario and on the St. Lawrence River cannot complain if they have the average reading they have had for 105 years. But when we start to give them a reading during the navigation season which is as low as 244 feet, two feet below average, and when in the wintertime we give them a reading of 243.07 feet, when as I say the average for 105 years has been 246 feet, then we are playing fast and loose with the people who enjoy a priority right in the international treaty, a right which is being violated every day of the year, every month of the year, year after year for the past several years. The first use is for domestic and sanitary purposes; the second use is for navigation; and the third use for power and irrigation purposes, Mr. Speaker.
The more I speak on this question of low water levels in Lake Ontario, occasioned by the water which is drawn off for power purposes, the more I am accused of wishing to hurt Ontario because I wish to restrict the amount of power development. I am not in the slightest hurting Ontario in demanding that the international treaty be observed and that the people who are given first priority in the treaty should enjoy the right that is theirs to use this water primarily for domestic and sanitary purposes.
The water power in the St. Lawrence River goes through three interesting hands. At the Cornwall power house one half goes to the Ontario Hydro Authority, the other half to the New York State Power Authority, which is the name of the organization which takes their power at Cornwall. Downstream you have the Cedars powerhouse on the St. Lawrence and the Beauharnois powerhouse, both owned by the Quebec Hydro Power Commission. So you have three power developers interested in getting as much water as they can out of Lake Ontario in order to develop power to sell to their customers.
When people in the basin of Lake Ontario who are anxious to see the minimum figure of 246 feet above sea level maintained the
May 11, 1965

year round-because it has been the average for 105 years-say to the authorities that they should not let the water level go down to 243.07 feet in the wintertime and 244 feet in the summertime during navigation season, they ask us what we will do about power, and ask us to think about the power we lose by not being able to suck the water off Lake Ontario. To which we simply reply that they can impose restrictions on the use of power and in that way reduce the demand. There is certainly no requirement on the power interests that they shall rob the people in the basin of Lake Ontario of water in order that they can sell horsepower here or a horsepower there, or take on a big commercial block contract on the United States side, or in Quebec or in Ontario.
One of the original proverbs of all time is that you cut your coat according to your cloth, an adage first printed in 1546 in the sayings of John Hey wood. Why cannot we develop the power in the international section of the St. Lawrence according to the water that is available to us? This should be used not primarily for the development of power, but to meet the everlasting demand for a supply of water. Many people talk about the use of water to provide power to operate electric stoves, razors, and other electrical appliances, but let me remind hon. Members that we have done without all these things in the past, and that there is a more important need.

There must be a more reasonable judgment of the values of the water in the Great Lakes. The attitude that people display in respect of the control of the water in the Great Lakes, and particularly in Lake Ontario, is one of constant amazement to me. There is supposedly a control dam at Iroquois, which is within 60 miles of Ottawa. At that point there is a great sign which refers to this control. It is at the locks and states:

This sign appears over the name of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, but having made some inquiries I am informed that the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority has no control in this regard.
This sign should read, "this lock is required for ships to by-pass the Iroquois dam which could control the level of Lake Ontario." I have gone by this Iroquois dam on scores of occasions and I have yet to see the gates closed. I have never seen the gates 22620-77 J

Water Levels of Great Lakes completely closed, but on one occasion I saw them about one third down, but not more.
Mr. Speaker, we have the means of controlling the flow of water downstream from Lake Ontario, and it is high time the Government told the International Joint Commission to instruct the International Joint River Board to control this level at a set minimum. The average level of water in Lake Ontario, over a period of 105 years, is 246 feet. If they are instructed to bring that level higher, even to that which it has been, 249 feet, all they have to do is let those gates down. This should be done, and this wastage of water should not be allowed, because of the interests of the millions of people who reside in the basin of Lake Ontario.

Lake Ontario, which holds Montreal's water, got the least of all.
It is surprising to me that the people of Montreal would consider the water in Lake Ontario as theirs. I suggest that the people who live on the shores of Lake Ontario should be able to enjoy this lake and consider it as their water, at least until they allow it to rush downstream unchecked to the Atlantic Ocean.
It must be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that the water from Lake Ontario rushes down the St. Lawrence River past the City of Montreal at the rate of 205,000 cubic feet a second on its way to the wide Atlantic. Many people in this country talk about the amount of water used by Chicago. The consumption of Great Lakes water by this tremendous city is in the neighbourhood of 3,100 cubic feet per second-1,500 feet for sewage purposes and 1,600 feet for navigation purposes. Let us consider at the same time that water rushes down the St. Lawrence past Montreal at the rate of 205,000 feet per second, in order to flush Montreal's
May 11, 1965

Water Levels of Great Lakes untreated sewage downstream. That is a project which requires a great deal of water. No effort is made whatsoever to control the flow of water at the east end of Montreal Island. If there was any desire to control the flow, a dam could be built. But instead of a dam to build up a harbour depth desired by the people of Montreal, they are now building a tunnel and a bridge at Boucher-ville, neither of which will impede the flow of the St. Lawrence River to the broad Atlantic.
I see no reason for allowing the water from Lake Ontario, which is important to that city, to the harbour of Hamilton, to Port Weller, to Kingston and other major centres along the St. Lawrence, to be released without control for downstream flow. I suggest that it is for this very reason that the rule to which I have referred regarding the various values of water was established. Surely there is not much point to any attempt to maintain water levels at the acceptable level of 246 feet in Lake Ontario while at the same time expecting this tremendous amount of water to rush downstream unchecked. In this regard one must remember that 205,000 cubic feet per second rushing past Montreal represents a sufficient quantity of water in one month to supply all the municipalities of Ontario, for a year.
As an example of what I am suggesting, let me point out that the City of London, England, has the greatest impounded body of water in the world. During high tide the boats tie up in locks, with a water depth level of 25 to 40 feet, and remain there until the return of the tide. They then proceed on their way at high tide. This same situation occurs in respect of Rotterdam and Antwerp. No one can convince me that this same practice could not be followed in relation to the City of Montreal, so far as usages and levels of water are concerned. At the present time this water is allowed to pass by the Iroquois dam without stopping. In my opinion that as it is now operated is a useless structure.
I think the people in authority should follow established precedent, and regard the waters of Ontario for the following purposes, in order of importance: domestic and health purposes first, navigation second and power third. Many people will say that what is good for the power interests is good for Ontario. And this is similar to what they tried to say in the United States, namely that what is good for General Motors is good for the United States. I say that many millions of


people in the United States maintained that the truth is that what is good for the United States is good for General Motors. And I say that what is good for Canada is good for the power interests. Mr. Speaker, let me say to you that there is no better maxim than that which states, "waste not, want not". In this regard let me quote a four-line quatrain written by Rowland Howard as follows:
Waste not, want not, is a maxim I would teach.
Let your watchword be dispatch, and practise what you preach:
Do not let your chances like sunbeams pass you by,
For you never miss the water till the well runs dry.
This quatrain appeared in Peterson's Magazine in 1876.
Let me say that if the dam at Iroquois is not used in order to control the water, the water level in Lake Ontario will not be maintained and the well will run dry very shortly. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest it is the responsibility of the Department of Transport and the Board of Transport Commissioners to order at once an inquiry into this situation. I have before me a great deal of correspondence from people in Vancouver, Calgary, Medicine Hat, Winnipeg and many other points along the line, complaining that they have waited three days, five days, in fact up to six weeks during which they have been denied reservations on C.P.R. passenger trains, yet at the same time the company is taking the kind of action that will further curtail this service.
One of the reasons why we must deal with this thing at once is that under the provisions of the Railway Act the C.P.R. is not required to receive permission from the Board of Transport Commissioners to reduce service, but it must have permission from the Board to abandon service. Every time it reduces service and reduces the amount of revenue derived from a particular train, the C.P.R. has a new bench mark of revenue against essentially the same level of expenses, and it uses this in its argument to the Board to allow it to abandon a service completely.

The argument keeps coming up that the air lines are taking over the job of moving passengers across Canada, but I suggest the air lines will soon be in a position where it will not be convenient for them to carry passengers except for distances of 300 to 500 miles and more. It is essential therefore that sufficient train passenger service be maintained to take care of the demand. In addition, many people in Canada do not like to fly, yet they want to travel across the country. Highway and bus services are adequate for some months of the year, but they are not as convenient and as comfortable as railroads for travelling during the winter months.
I hope the Minister, the Department or the Board will order an investigation into these rumours that the C.P.R. is going to curtail further its railway passenger service, so that we can find out how much demand there is for this kind of service and see whether or not the railways are doing what is necessary to make sure it is being provided.

There is provision in the Railway Act to see that this service is supplied. In addition to the information that the railway has been providing up to this point, respecting the number of passengers carried, the railroads should also be required to provide the Board of Transport Commissioners with the number of requests they receive for railway passenger service. I say so because if you accept only 65 or 90-whatever the day coach carries- and turn down another 130 requests, and do not list them, you do not give an adequate or correct reflection of the demand for this kind of service. I would hope immediate action will be taken because during the ensuing months there will be an increased demand for this kind of passenger service, and by all the indications the C.P.R. is going to decrease this service rather than increase it in keeping with public demand.

maintopic: EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR INCREASED PER CAPITA GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES
EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR INCREASED PER CAPITA GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to participate in a debate at this hour of night. However, the needs of the universities of this country cannot be interfered with, I think, and a minute or two to bring this matter to the attention of the Government once again will, I hope, be useful. The problem I face, of course, is that there is such a mass of information about the problem facing our universities in Canada today that it is rather difficult to boil it all down into a minute or two.
The Minister of Finance in his Budget, when referring to federal assistance to universities, said that he and his colleagues were prepared to wait until the results of the study being made by the Bladen Commission were brought down. The Bladen Commission was set up by a private group, the Canadian Universities Foundation, and financed-this is part of the Canadian paradox-by United States and Canadian corporations. The C.U.F. asked the Minister of Finance in December 1963 to increase per capita grants for universities in this country. As a matter of fact, the first brief was submitted to the Prime Minister in May of 1963, and one of the mysteries of this Government-at least I consider it a mystery-so far as assistance to universities in this country is concerned is that they have done absolutely nothing since the time they assumed office to the present day.
Dr. John Deutsch, who is featured in the May issue of the Atlantic Advocate, an issue which concerned itself largely with education for national growth, had something to say about this. After all, Dr. Deutsch is Chairman of the Economic Council of Canada. He recommended that the contribution of the Federal Government be increased by $2 to $3 per head of population. He goes on to say:
A rapid and sustained expansion of university education, including education at the postgraduate level, must be given a high priority in making available the necessary resources in comparison with other forms of public expenditure.
May 11, 1965

He adds:
There has long been a deficiency in our educational system in regard to the training of technical personnel beyond the high school but short of the university level. The value of our natural wealth is great, but. .. there are even greater riches in the knowledge and skills of men.
It is not often, Mr. Speaker, that a Government is given both the problem and the answer to the problem in such simple, clear and readily understandable terms. After all, the problem is that the universities of Canada are receiving grossly inadequate amounts of money from the federal Government. The answer to this problem, or a good deal of it, is contained in the submission of the Canadian Universities Foundation made to the Minister of Finance in December 1963, and is as follows:
University operating costs are rising at a rate greater than 16 per cent per annum. The chief contributing factors are:
(1)	Enrolment of full time students is going up at an average of between 11 and 12 per cent per annum;
(2)	Additional university teachers are being appointed each year, and their salary rates are rising;
(3)	As more buildings are provided to accommodate students and staff, maintenance costs increase;
(4)	Facilities for graduate studies and research are being expanded, and these are costly to operate.
Effective for the fiscal year 1962-63, the then Government of Canada increased the sum available for university grants by raising the rate per capita of the population of the province to $2. Including allotments, direct or indirect, for all ten provinces, the grants totalled $37 million in that year. If the federal Government contribution to the operating costs of the universities had kept pace with the rise in those costs, the total sum available for 1963-64 would have been $43 million.
I interpolate at this point, Mr. Speaker, that I understand that as of now the amount of money would be some $58 million.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
As I say, the problem I have is to try to digest the tremendous amount of evidence now available to the Government concerning what has been rightly classified as a crisis.
I am trying to boil it down and make a presentation to a Government which up to now has done nothing about this crisis since it assumed office. And they have the answer. The Canadian Universities Foundation in its brief has presented the Government with the answer. Dr. Deutsch, the Chairman of the Government's own Economic Council, has supplied the answer. Members of Parliament have tried during the months to provide this answer. I think it is deplorable for the Minister to slough off his obvious responsibility in the manner in which he has done. The

ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-REPORT OF LAW SOCIETY RESPECTING ONTARIO SUPREME COURT JUDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel about as nervous as a maiden speaker, because I have never spoken in the House at such a late hour.
1190	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I asked the Minister the following question: Has the Minister received, and has he had time to examine, communications from the Law Society of Upper Canada about the position of Hon. Mr. Justice Landreville, a Justice of the Supreme Court of Ontario; what is the nature of the communication received, and what, if anything, does he intend to do about this situation which has cast a shadow over the administration of justice.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit my surprise when I heard the ruling made by Mr. Speaker, that this was a question for the Order Paper. My surprise was occasioned partially by the fact that a similar question asked a few days ago was allowed but the Minister at that time had not yet had time to examine the communication. My surprise was heightened because I thought anything that affected the integrity of the administration of justice was of the highest urgency.
I need hardly tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the Benchers of the Law Society of Upper Canada are the governing authority of all members of the Bar of Ontario. This body has the reputation which one would expect of the senior leaders of the Bar-a reputation of extreme caution, particularly in respect of matters affecting the reputation of the judiciary.
It is my understanding that the Law Society did something unprecedented in the legal history of Ontario about a week or two ago, when it was announced in a press report that the Benchers of the Law Society concerned had sent a report concerning Mr. Justice Landreville to the Minister of Justice. What I want to know and what I think this House should want to know is whether this responsible, and I might almost say ultra respectable body indicated in their report that there was any reason for the very grave disquiet that many have felt about this situation.
The activities of this judge shortly before he was appointed to the Bench have been revealed by a series of investigations and trials. I will not attempt to outline them here. It is only fair to point out that in criminal proceedings it was held by a magistrate that there was no case for criminal trial on the charges laid. But the standard expected of a justice of the Supreme Court is not just the standard of avoiding the application of
DEBATES	May 11, 1965
the criminal law. What is complained of here may not be within the purview of the Criminal Code but it still might be a matter unbecoming one who occupies high judicial office. In any event, I think this House is entitled to know whether or not the Benchers of the Law Society have made a report which either directly or indirectly suggests that action should be taken by the Minister or by this House in regard to the matter.
It is my conviction, Mr. Speaker, that the absolute integrity of the judiciary is one of the most important pillars in the whole fabric of our judicial system and, indeed, of our whole democratic system. I trust the Minister will leave no stone unturned to make sure that justice in Canada is above reproach. I look forward to a direct answer from the Minister or from his Parliamentary Secretary.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-REPORT OF LAW SOCIETY RESPECTING ONTARIO SUPREME COURT JUDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can say on behalf of the Minister that in fact a report has been received from the Benchers of the Law Society of Upper Canada in connection with the matter to which the hon. Member has referred. I am advised that the report followed a letter which arrived two days before marked "private and confidential" and that the Minister assumed that this applied to the report. It is for that reason that the contents have not been revealed.
Following upon receipt of the report the Minister took steps to advise Mr. Justice Landreville to the effect that it had been communicated to him and invited Mr. Justice Landreville to express his own views on the question. These are expected from the judge either late this week or early next week.
The hon. Member has said that he feels that justice in Canada should be above reproach, a general principle with which I think no one will disagree. I am sure that hon. Members will agree that before any decision or action on this particular question is taken both viewpoints on the question should be heard. Therefore I think any statement should be deferred and that we should await the response from the judge which, as I have indicated, is expected late this week or early next week.

subtopic: PRESS RELEASE RESPECTING RUSSIAN ESPIONAGE ACTIVITIES

speechtext:
Saturday, May 8, 1965
The Department of External Affairs today announced that the Ambassador of the Soviet Union was requested on May 4 to arrange for the departure from Canada of two members of his mission, Mr. A. E. Bytchkov, of the commercial section, and a chancery clerk, Mr. V. N. Poluchkin. The Canadian Government had learned that they had engaged in activities incompatible with their official status and had, therefore, found it necessary to declare them persona non grata. They left Canada on May 7.
In one instance a Canadian civil servant was paid thousands of dollars to gather information and documentation in Canada, the purpose of which was to assist in the establishment of espionage activities in Canada and in other countries, and to perform economic intelligence tasks, including the provision of detailed information on the Trans-
Mountain Pipe Line system in Western Canada.
In another instance a naturalized Canadian citizen was paid thousands of dollars to provide technical information in the electronics field related to defence industry and to compromise other Canadians, including female employees of the Government, with the object of securing their assistance in obtaining access to classified information. He was given specialized photographic training to assist him in these tasks.
The approaches made by the two members of the Soviet Embassy very shortly came to the attention of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As a result of this co-operation by conscientious Canadians, the police were able to establish the improper intent of the Soviet approaches and to put an end to them before any damage was done to Canadian interests.
Wednesday, May 12, 1965
